plain_text:
The researchers in the Library's magnificent
Main Reading Room toil away under the
watchful eye of Father Time, looking
down from atop a massive clock over the
entrance.
semantic_text: The researchers in the Library's magnificent Main Reading Room toil away under the watchful eye of Father Time, looking down from atop a massive clock over the entrance.

plain_text:
The clock serves as more than just a way
to tell time. It's also an extraordinary work
of art – a combination of practical function,
inspired design, rich decoration and years of
sweat.
semantic_text: The clock serves as more than just a way to tell time. It's also an extraordinary work of art – a combination of practical function, inspired design, rich decoration and years of sweat.

plain_text:
It sits in a frame of multicolored marbles,
inset with semiprecious stones and flanked
by golden-flamed torches. The gilt face
of the dial, which measures about 4 feet
across, represents brilliant bursts of sunlight.
semantic_text: It sits in a frame of multicolored marbles, inset with semiprecious stones and flanked by golden-flamed torches. The gilt face of the dial, which measures about 4 feet across, represents brilliant bursts of sunlight.

plain_text:
A bronze sculpture of Father Time strides
above, moving relentlessly forward like time
itself. In his hands, he carries an hourglass
and a scythe – a reminder to mortals that
their own time on Earth is passing.
semantic_text: A bronze sculpture of Father Time strides above, moving relentlessly forward like time itself. In his hands, he carries an hourglass and a scythe – a reminder to mortals that their own time on Earth is passing.

plain_text:
The clock was the creation of young sculptor
John Flanagan and took seven years to
finish – much to the exasperation of Bernard
Green, construction superintendent for
the Library's new Jefferson Building. The
Jefferson opened to the public in November
1897 to great acclaim. The last pieces of the
clock, however, weren't installed until nearly
five years later – finally, Green wrote in his
journal, making the building complete.
semantic_text: The clock was the creation of young sculptor John Flanagan and took seven years to finish – much to the exasperation of Bernard Green, construction superintendent for the Library's new Jefferson Building. The Jefferson opened to the public in November 1897 to great acclaim. The last pieces of the clock, however, weren't installed until nearly five years later – finally, Green wrote in his journal, making the building complete.

plain_text:
Flanagan went on to design a work familiar
to every American who ever fished in a
pocket for change: the U.S. quarter with the
left-facing profile of George Washington on
one side and a spread-winged eagle on the
other, first issued in 1932.
semantic_text: Flanagan went on to design a work familiar to every American who ever fished in a pocket for change: the U.S. quarter with the left-facing profile of George Washington on one side and a spread-winged eagle on the other, first issued in 1932.

plain_text:
Today, his great clock remains an
extraordinary feature in a space filled with
the extraordinary – and, to the researchers
working below, a reminder of deadlines
drawing ever nearer.
semantic_text: Today, his great clock remains an extraordinary feature in a space filled with the extraordinary – and, to the researchers working below, a reminder of deadlines drawing ever nearer.

plain_text:
■ John Flanagan's original design (bottom) contained
detailed notes on materials and placement. The
snake hands shown in the drawing were not included
in the final version (top). Prints and Photographs
Division, Manuscript Division

visual_description:
The image displays two distinct sections: an ornate sculptural clock above and a technical drawing below. The upper section features bronze figures including a central winged figure holding a scythe, flanked by seated nude figures, set against a gold mosaic background with marble columns on either side. The clock face has Roman numerals and decorative hands.

The lower section is a hand-drawn architectural or design sketch of the same clock’s front elevation, annotated with material specifications in red ink such as “JADE OR MALACHITE,” “RED GREEK MARBLE,” “GILT SUN / SHINE,” “VIRGIN H. BRONZE,” and “A SERPENT HANDS BLACK GRANITE.” The drawing includes structural details like pilasters, a sunburst motif behind the dial, and labeled components indicating materials for different parts of the clock’s frame and ornamentation.
